Configured or registered credentials and known sensitive representations are withheld from unnecessary agent/process inputs and redacted from controlled outputs; untrusted attachments and repository data are handled without implicitly treating them as safe.
Verification evidence identifies checked channels and secret forms; passing known-secret redaction cases does not prove arbitrary unknown or transformed secrets can never appear.
Each project independently selects its GitHub authentication method.
GitHub App authentication is preferred but not required.
Personal access tokens remain a supported authentication option.
Task execution, Git operations, logging, persistent state, and restart recovery work in both environments.
Runtime paths are configurable rather than tied to container-specific directories.
Docker is not required for normal local operation.
Setup runs only for the appropriate project and worktree, never in the original checkout.
For refinement, setup-generated files are tracked as setup effects; the refinement agent remains read-only with respect to repository content.
Setup results and failures are captured separately from structured orchestrator logs and handled safely.

Failed or timed-out configured setup prevents starting the agent, retains work and diagnostics, and receives bounded recovery; unrecoverable pre-PR setup produces a verified task failure, while post-PR setup failure retains the open PR and project ownership as a reported operational blockage.

Setup-produced tracked changes are independently attributed; implementation commits contain only reviewed task-relevant changes, while unrelated changes are preserved without silent deletion or unsafe publication.
A completed setup is not unnecessarily repeated after task recovery.
When setup is unconfigured, the orchestrator records that it was skipped.
Refinement, planning, implementation, independent review, remediation, and commit-message generation can each have project-specific model and variant settings.
Missing model or variant settings defer to OpenCode's own configured defaults.
An explicitly configured but unavailable model is reported rather than silently replaced.
Supported documents, images, and logs attached to the card can be accessed during refinement and implementation.
Attachments are refreshed when work starts or resumes, rather than silently relying on stale context.
Downloaded attachment data is kept outside repository worktrees and access failures are reported.
The agent evaluates the task description, repository, and attachments before requesting clarification.
If essential information cannot be inferred reliably, the card moves to `Failed` with an actionable Trello comment identifying what is missing.
The user may clarify the card and explicitly return it to `Ready for Agent` for a fresh attempt.
Implementation, validation, reviews, CI repair, and PR maintenance do not modify the Trello card title or description.
Trello comments describe meaningful outcomes or attention needs, not routine validation, reviews, or retries.
Fine-grained progress and diagnostic details remain in execution logs instead of cluttering the card.
The orchestrator preserves execution state and pauses the affected project rather than assuming the manual move completed its workflow.
Returning the card to its expected list can trigger automatic resumption after safety verification.
Unrelated projects continue; any remaining uncertainty is reported and reconciled without destructive assumptions.
Tests verify complete paths from Trello task selection through implementation, PR delivery, human review, and terminal card outcomes.
Negative reviews, failing validation, exhaustion, crashes, restarts, and external interruptions are exercised as relevant to their requirements.
Unit-test success alone is not accepted as evidence that an entire workflow is correct.
End-to-end verification includes realistic integration of the complete task lifecycle, beyond solely mocked individual units.
Tests can simulate successful and failing responses from the relevant external services.
Simulated errors cover partial external success, timeouts, delayed or missing results, and recovery after restart.
Verification checks observable outcomes such as PR count, card state, preserved work, and bounded attempts rather than relying only on agent-reported success.
Stable requirement IDs can be referenced by later test scenarios, implementation audits, and correction tasks.
Verification distinguishes demonstrated behavior from untested, partial, or missing coverage.
The verification baseline includes realistic end-to-end workflow evidence in addition to mocked and unit tests; simulated service failures remain suitable for routine automated checks.
A dedicated live-service testing environment is a possible future improvement, not a prerequisite to addressing current robustness defects.
